We have p | 26q - 1, so 26q ≡ 1 (mod p), i.e., 26q - 1 = kp for some positive integer k.
And q | 26p + 1, so 26p ≡ -1 (mod q), i.e., 26p + 1 = mq for some positive integer m.

So 26q - 1 = kp and 26p + 1 = mq.

Multiply: (26q-1)(26p+1) = kmpq
26²pq + 26q - 26p - 1 = kmpq

So (676 - km)pq = 26(p - q) + 1.

Let n = km. Then (676 - n)pq = 26(p-q) + 1.

Since p, q are primes (positive, ≥2), pq ≥ 4. The right side 26(p-q)+1 could be positive, negative, or zero.

Case analysis on n = km.

If p = q: then p | 26p - 1 means p | 1, so p = 1, not prime. So p ≠ q.

Let me think about bounds. k = (26q-1)/p, m = (26p+1)/q.

Since p, q ≥ 2: k = (26q-1)/p. If p is large relative to q, k small.

Let me consider the equation (676 - n)pq = 26(p - q) + 1 where n = km ≥ 1.

The RHS: |26(p-q)+1|. If p > q, RHS positive; if p < q, RHS could be negative (when 26(q-p) > 1, i.e., q > p basically always for primes ≥2... well 26(q-p) ≥ 26 so RHS = 26(p-q)+1 = -26(q-p)+1 < 0).

So if p < q: RHS < 0, so (676 - n) < 0 (since pq > 0), thus n > 676.
If p > q: RHS = 26(p-q)+1 > 0, so n < 676.

Case 1: p > q. Then n = km < 676.
Case 2: p < q. Then n > 676.

Let me bound k and m. 

k = (26q - 1)/p. m = (26p + 1)/q.

km = (26q-1)(26p+1)/(pq) = (676pq + 26q - 26p - 1)/(pq) = 676 + (26q - 26p - 1)/(pq) = 676 + (26(q-p) - 1)/(pq).
